title: Business Management SL · Set B · Paper 2
subject: business-management

questions.title: Section A · Pierlight Prints
questions.stem: Pierlight sells posters at CU 15. Its variable cost per poster is CU 6 and its monthly fixed costs are CU 13,500. Monthly sales are 1,800 posters. A new printer would increase fixed costs by CU 2,700 per month and reduce variable cost to CU 4.50. Assume selling price and product quality stay the same.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate Pierlight’s current monthly profit and margin of safety in units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the monthly sales volume at which profit would be the same with either printer.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two reasons why management might keep the current printer even if its sales forecast exceeds this volume.

steps.text: Current contribution is CU 9 per poster.
Break-even output is 13,500/9 = 1,500.
Margin of safety is 300 posters.
Equate the CU 2,700 additional fixed cost with the CU 1.50 saving per unit.
1,800 posters.
A forecast could overstate sales.
Monthly sales below 1,800 leave the business with the higher fixed cost and insufficient variable savings.
Installation or staff training could interrupt production.
Lost sales or delivery penalties could outweigh the forecast profit gain. Accept other contextual risks.

questions.title: Section A · Mira Fieldwear
questions.stem: Mira had opening inventory of CU 12,000, purchases of CU 64,000 and closing inventory of CU 16,000. Annual sales revenue was CU 100,000 and other operating expenses CU 27,000. A retailer will accept supplies only on 60-day credit.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct an extract of the income statement showing cost of sales, gross profit and operating profit.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the operating profit margin. Explain why an increase in this margin need not remove a shortage of cash.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one way Mira could reduce the cash tied up in inventory and one risk of doing so.

steps.text: Opening inventory plus purchases less closing inventory.
Cost of sales is CU 60,000.
Gross profit is CU 40,000.
Operating profit is CU 13,000.
Credit sales can be recognised before cash is received.
The retailer can delay receipts for 60 days while wages and suppliers still need payment.
Order smaller batches more frequently or align purchasing to demand.
The lower inventory balance releases cash.
A delay could cause stockouts and lost orders from the retailer.

questions.title: Section B · Option 1 · Northbank Music
questions.stem: Northbank offers evening lessons. Each place costs the school CU 14 in instructor time and earns CU 32 in fees. Each term it sells 800 places, with fixed costs of CU 11,400. Offering 200 online places would add CU 2,400 in fixed costs. Online places sell for CU 28 and have a variable cost of CU 10. The director estimates that 60 current in-person places would be replaced by online bookings. Parents report uneven internet access.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate Northbank’s existing operating profit per term.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the change in term profit from the online proposal and the minimum number of online places needed to cover its extra costs if 60 in-person bookings are lost.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two qualitative factors that could affect the decision.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether to launch online lessons for the full term.

steps.text: CU 120 increase.
At least 194 online places.
Some families have unreliable internet.
Disrupted lessons may harm retention or the school’s reputation.
Others cannot travel in the evening.
Remote delivery could expand access to customers the school currently misses.

The proposal offers more access but only CU 120 expected additional profit. Six fewer online places would reduce this by CU 108, and seven would turn the gain negative. Test prepaid demand, monitor transfers from in-person lessons and retain an accessible offline option. A school prioritising access might accept a modest return if it can protect quality and cover the fixed platform cost. Use best fit. Credit a well-supported alternative.

questions.title: Section B · Option 2 · Grey Heron Foods
questions.stem: Grey Heron has a monthly cash balance of CU 9,000 before opening a kiosk. It expects the kiosk to collect CU 18,000 and pay CU 15,000 operating costs each month for three months. Installation costs CU 10,000 at the start of month 1. The business must keep at least CU 3,000 available at all times. The landlord offers instalments of CU 5,400 at the start of months 1 and 2 instead. Assume operating net inflows arrive at each month-end and no other cash movements.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the opening-month balance immediately after paying the full installation cost and the month-end balance.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Under the instalment plan, calculate the balances immediately after each instalment and the balance at the end of month 3.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two reasons actual monthly net inflows might differ from the forecast.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Recommend whether Grey Heron should proceed under either offer.

steps.text: Immediately −CU 1,000.
Month-end CU 2,000.
Month 1 after instalment CU 3,600.
End of month 1 is CU 6,600, carried into month 2.
Month 2 after instalment CU 1,200.
End of month 3 is CU 7,200.
New footfall or conversion rates may differ from expected demand.
Fewer sales reduce cash receipts.
Ingredient prices or staffing hours may rise.
Higher cash operating costs reduce the expected CU 3,000 surplus.

Paying immediately puts the balance CU 4,000 below the floor. Instalments preserve more early cash but still leave month 2 CU 1,800 short of the floor and cost CU 800 extra. Seek a later second instalment or a confirmed credit facility and reassess pessimistic demand. Three profitable months alone do not ensure liquidity on payment dates. Deferring is defensible if financing is uncertain. Use best fit.
